result:
Neither. "More agents always give better results" isn't true, so five versus ten is the wrong question.

Anthropic measured this on their own multi-agent research system. A lead agent with several subagents beat a single agent on their internal research eval. But agents used about 4× the tokens of a chat, and multi-agent systems about 15×. They say this only pays off when the task is valuable enough to cover the cost ([source](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)). Their guidance on agents in general is to start with the simplest solution and add complexity only when it falls short ([source](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents)).

Here is that applied to your makerspace assistant. A student asks, "Can I use the laser cutter Thursday at 3? I haven't done the training."

- Answering from a manual, checking the calendar and booking a slot are three tools. One agent with three well-described tools can do all of it.
- Ten agents would each need their own context and instructions. They would also pass messages between themselves, and every one of those steps costs tokens. On a small budget, that cost is the main risk.
- Splitting starts to pay off when the work can run in parallel and a single context gets too crowded. For example, searching many long manuals at once could justify it. A booking question rarely does.
- Some steps may not need an agent at all. Checking training status and then booking is a fixed sequence, so a plain workflow in your Python code can do it for less.

I haven't taught multi-agent systems yet, so this is the short version. You can also use it at your design review: start with one agent, and name the specific failure that would make you add a second.

Quick check: in the laser cutter example, which step could be plain code instead of an agent, and why?

I can write a lesson on workflows versus agents, and then one on when multiple agents pay off, if you'd like.

Sources:
- [How we built our multi-agent research system](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/multi-agent-research-system)
- [Building effective agents](https://www.anthropic.com/research/building-effective-agents)
